abstract: Q3 2026 observation of the Real-Time Population Survey generative AI module, published as FRED series RPSGENAIUSAGESHAREWORK and on the authors' own GenAI Adoption Tracker as the August 2026 wave. The series measures the share of employed US adults aged 18-64 who use generative AI for work, from a nationally representative online labour market survey fielded quarterly by Alexander Bick, Adam Blandin and David Deming since August 2024. It is the cleanest worker-side adoption series in the field and the series jobsdata.ai plots on genai-work-adoption. FRED updated the series on October 20, 2026.
keyFindings: Work adoption fell to 40.5 percent in Q3 2026 from 45.2 percent in Q2 2026, a drop of 4.65 points. This is the first quarterly decline since Q4 2024 (31.0 percent from 33.3 percent) and the largest in the series.
Overall adoption among adults 18-64 fell much less, to 60.8 percent from 61.8 percent, a decline of 1.0 point, so the fall is concentrated in the work question rather than in genAI use generally.

The two intensity measures moved the same way: GenAI-assisted work hours fell to 5.3 percent of total work hours from 6.3 percent (RPSGENAIASSISTWRKHRSALL), and reported time saved fell to 2.1 percent from 2.2 percent (RPSGENAITSALL).
Neither FRED nor the GenAI Adoption Tracker publishes any note explaining the decline, and no methodology revision is described for this wave.
The Q1 2026 readings were also revised down from the July 2026 FRED vintage: work adoption 43.4 to 42.8 percent, overall adoption 57.9 to 57.6 percent.
Before this wave the series had risen for seven consecutive quarters, from 32.7 percent in Q1 2025 to 45.2 percent in Q2 2026.
methodology: The Real-Time Population Survey is a nationally representative online survey of US working-age adults aged 18-64, designed and weighted to be nationally representative, fielded quarterly since August 2024. The work-adoption question is 'Do you use Generative AI for your job?', asked of employed respondents, so the denominator is employed adults rather than all adults. FRED publishes the module as 137 quarterly series (category 8) with industry and occupation breakdowns, dating each observation to the start of the quarter; the authors' tracker labels the same wave by its field month, which for Q3 2026 is August 2026. jobsdata.ai dates these points to the field month, which is how the prior six waves in the chart are dated. The citation the authors request is 'The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI', Bick, Blandin and Deming, Management Science (2026).
qualifiers: A single quarterly wave, and a 4.65-point fall is large against the series' own history of 2 to 3 point quarterly moves, so it should be read as provisional until the next wave either confirms a plateau or reverses it. Two readings make the decline harder to dismiss as pure noise - the intensity measures fell alongside the adoption rate - but two readings also do not establish a turn. The divergence between the work rate (-4.65) and the overall rate (-1.0) is unexplained by the publisher and could reflect a composition change in the employed subsample rather than workers abandoning the tools. Self-reported use at a low threshold, so it measures reach, not how much work AI performs.
